entry.title: Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B
entry.content:
Introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: Powering Agentic Coding and Private Knowledge Work

Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads.

With Ternary Bonsai 2 27B, we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately.

Agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an important milestone in improving the intelligence density of models.

We evaluated Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B against both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full-precision Qwen 3.8 27B base model, as reported in the full whitepaper. We see marked improvements in agentic execution, coding, and multi-turn tool use, as shown in the table below.

On a single NVIDIA H100, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieves a generation speed of 291 tokens/s with MTP and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s. Even on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, it delivers 204 tokens/s with MTP and a prompt processing speed of approximately 3,060 tokens/s. The demos below follow complete local workflows, from the initial request through intermediate decisions to the final result.

For products, this creates room to build assistance directly into the applications where work already happens: a coding assistant working through issues in a private repository, a document application that prepares reviewable summaries, or a desktop assistant that handles recurring analysis. Local deployment lets those products process sensitive material on the user’s device. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical.

Platform Coverage

Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices (Mac, iPhone, iPad) via MLX.

Model weights are available today under the Apache 2.0 License.

Full technical details of our compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in our whitepaper.

Work with Us

We work with teams to tailor Bonsai models to their applications, from post-training on domain-specific data to optimizing inference for target hardware. If you’re building AI products with tight memory, latency, or power requirements, we’d love to explore how Bonsai can help. Reach out at sales@prismml.com.

Join Us

PrismML emerged from a team of Caltech researchers and was founded with support from Khosla Ventures, Cerberus, and Google, with continuing support from Samsung. We've spent years tackling one of the field's hardest problems: compressing neural networks without sacrificing their reasoning ability.

If you want to help build the next generation of state-of-the-art AI, we'd love to hear from you. Check out our careers page.

entry.title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
entry.content:
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

With our research partner, Onava(opens in a new window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study(opens in a new window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

For three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.

Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both showed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.

The unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

Researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design new loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.

We started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design new sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.

We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.

Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a new enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.

We tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench(opens in a new window), including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding.

For each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold(opens in a new window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.

In a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.

In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH(opens in a new window), a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.

Many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.

We counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.

Many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.

For our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset(opens in a new window), a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.

In practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt. We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset(opens in a new window), where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions(opens in a new window), and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock(opens in a new window) reached 60%.

Where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we showed the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.

With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.

Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.

We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.

We drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.

In one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.

In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.

Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.

The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.

What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.

It is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.

Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.

Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.

The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.

This work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

Find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.

Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

Design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.

As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.

While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

2026

entry.title: PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches
entry.content:
PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches

A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson.

The text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude. I plan to rewrite it in my own words over Thanksgiving Break but needed to get the project out. So apologies for this move - all of my other posts were written by me, and all future posts will be as well. Even if you find Claude more comprehensible than my meandering thoughts, meander nonetheless I shall.

Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad.

So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt.

Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected.

How it works

That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture.

The data

Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive.

The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them.

Training a model

I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Here are the rows I found most interesting; the paper has the rest.

Handwriting Score change Style rank Legible Graves-style LSTM, same tokens +0.029 2.2 49% ScribeTokens BPE, 60x the vocabulary −0.001 1.9 53% PenGPT 0.716 1.9 54% A tenth of the data +0.050 3.0 47% No augmentation +0.028 2.0 52% One word per sequence +0.009 6.0 52% No pen position +0.001 1.9 52% No BPE merges −0.010 – 55% Twice the parameters −0.004 1.9 55% Real ink 66%
Drawings Score change Matches label Matches caption sketch-rnn-style LSTM, same tokens +0.049 40% 20% Trained on Quick, Draw! only +0.002 74% 37% PenGPT 0.591 76% 43% No augmentation +0.013 4% 6% No pen position +0.008 74% 40% Half the layers, half the width +0.022 62% 31%

Data and how you show it. Those are the big rows. Cut the data and everything gets worse. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0.

The clever parts barely register. Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly worse; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing.

Even the transformer is optional, sort of. An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up new hands. On drawings, where sequences are several times longer, it falls well behind.

Samples

Enough tables. Here’s what the two models make.

The drawing model takes a few controls besides the prompt. One of them is how much ink to use.

It can also draw some things it was never shown as long as a blend of two familiar ideas will do.

Picking up a new hand

The trick is almost embarrassingly simple. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. No style encoder, no fine-tuning. That’s how the 21 hands at the top of this post were written.

It also works from a photo. There are no strokes in a photo so I trace a few of its words with InkSight and fit one new writer vector to the traces, with the rest of the model frozen.

Reading the letters

One head in layer 4 puts 81% of its attention on the letter being written. I looked for heads that specialize in cursive or print and found none; every head reads the same positions in both.

Do you need captions?

Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?

You can’t. The picture-only model has the best likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).

What it can’t do

The drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.

Closing thoughts

If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in The Bitter Lesson. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.

I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My previous attempt, the Cursive Transformer, took upwards of 10 hours on an A100 and only ever learned one hand. The tokenizer I used here is much simpler and far less elegant but it just works.

The bitter lesson kills or sidelines a lot of beautiful research ideas. It’s like gravity: it constrains you and most of the time it’s a very bad idea to fight back. But as I accept it and begin to work with it, I find things to admire. As a physicist I’m fascinated by the emerging science of scaling laws. And as a lover of biology I like the idea of putting a ton of work into the data and then literally growing a model on it, as you would an organism. Then you get to interact with it, learn what it’s capable of and study how it works. Seen this way, the bitter lesson has its own charm.

entry.title: Top open problems in mathematics ranked by LLM-assessed importance
entry.content:
The ProofAtlas ranking

Top 500 open problems in mathematicsranked by LLM-assessed importance

Explore questions in mathematics, computation, and mathematical physics, with exact statements, status notes, and sources.

This is a model-based assessment of mathematical importance, not an expert consensus or a forecast of which problems will be solved next.

Resolved problems from earlier editions remain available with their original ranks and sources.

2 entries have conditional ranks. Each entry explains why.

How the ranking works

What importance means here. Each entry is a specific mathematical question. Importance considers the significance of a resolution, centrality within its field, reach across fields, scholarly and historical fame, broader recognition, and scientific or practical impact.

How problems are ranked. LLMs compare pairs of problems. A reliability-weighted model combines those judgments into the ranking, with calibration across model families. The model-family weights are OpenAI 1.00, Claude 1.00, GLM 0.95, and DeepSeek 0.90. These are modeling choices, not measured probabilities of correctness.

What a rank means. Nearby ranks can be uncertain. The expanded entries include available ranking ranges and comparison counts. Filtering or alphabetizing the directory preserves every problem’s rank in this edition.

Diagnostics from the preceding source fit. After the reported resolutions, edition ranks were compacted without a new numerical fit. The displayed uncertainty ranges and comparison counts come from the preceding fit of 1,280 targets; the current eligible pool contains 1,122. These diagnostics were not recomputed for the smaller pool.

Related and nested problems. A substantial subproblem or generalization may receive its own rank when it has independent mathematical standing. Families identify narrow groups of related questions; an implication alone does not merge their families. The ranking process checks family crowding, including a diagnostic retaining the highest-ranked member of each family. Family membership does not itself change scores, impose a quota, or create an automatic penalty.

Dates and sources. The edition date identifies this list. A status review date, when recorded, appears separately inside each entry; it does not promise that the literature has been checked since then. Source links identify the exact formulation and available status evidence.

The ranking preserves a fixed edition. Separately dated status notes cover 176 of 500 entries; this is not a fresh literature review of the whole list. Recent resolution claims and formulation concerns are marked below with their historical ranks retained.

 Rank002Riemann HypothesisDo all zeros of the Riemann zeta function inside the strip with real part between zero and one lie exactly on its middle line?Number theory & arithmetic geometryRiemann hypotheses and exceptional zeros · 3 problemsExact statement

For the meromorphic continuation of the Riemann zeta function zeta(s)=sum_{n>=1} n^(-s), initially defined for Re(s)>1, every zero s in the open critical strip 0<Re(s)<1 has Re(s)=1/2. This is the Riemann Hypothesis for zeta alone; it does not assert simplicity of its zeros.

Why it matters

A proof would sharply control fluctuations in the distribution of primes: the prime-counting function would differ from its logarithmic-integral approximation by at most O(√x log x). A disproof would invalidate this equivalent error bound.

StatusOpen

Earlier note (2026-09-14): Riemann remains open. September 2026 progress on the proportion of simple critical-line zeros is partial, not proof that every nontrivial zero lies on the line. Uncorroborated or inaccessible proof claims were not accepted. October 7, 2026: OpenAI’s October 6 release reports partial progress. A zero-free half-plane Re(s)>7/8 for zeta excludes only the right-hand part of the critical strip. The target requires every nontrivial zero to have real part exactly 1/2; no conclusion excluding zeros between 1/2 and 7/8 is supplied. This is partial zero-location progress, not the Riemann Hypothesis. No independent proof audit or Lean verification was performed for this update.

 Rank003Yang-Mills Existence and Mass GapCan a nontrivial Yang–Mills quantum field theory in four-dimensional spacetime be constructed rigorously for every compact simple gauge group—the choice of internal symmetry—with a positive, finite gap between vacuum energy and the remaining energy spectrum?Mathematical physicsExact statement

For every compact simple gauge group G, prove that a nontrivial four-dimensional quantum Yang-Mills theory on R^4 exists with all existence requirements of Jaffe-Witten, Quantum Yang-Mills Theory, sections 3-4, including axiomatic properties at least as strong as their cited references [45,35], the required gauge-invariant local fields and short-distance compatibility specified there. The construction would turn the specified four-dimensional quantum gauge-field model into a theory satisfying the required mathematical axioms. Its spectrum would have a positive, finite gap above vacuum energy, without requiring an isolated first excited eigenstate.

The full existence-and-mass-gap target remains open. Earlier three-dimensional outlines, individual gauge-group claims and withdrawn postings also do not establish the full target. Earlier note (2026-09-14): BSD rank equality remains open. The located all-rank working-draft claim lacks independent acceptance; recent uses and special cases do not supply a universal proof. October 7, 2026: OpenAI’s October 6 release reports partial progress. The target is equality of analytic and Mordell-Weil ranks for every E/Q, rather than the full leading-term formula. This family gives that equality and the stronger leading-term conclusion when the full q-power Selmer corank is zero or one for some prime q. It leaves curves outside that hypothesis untreated, so it is a low-corank subcase only. The companion proves rank equality for E/Q with nonzero rational two-torsion and full 2-power Selmer corank zero or one, allowing arbitrary reduction at 2. The BSD rank target includes every E/Q without either restriction, so this is a limited subcase and does not follow as a full closure from the H10 result. The low-corank 2-converse explicitly gives equality of analytic and Mordell-Weil ranks for E/Q whose full 2-power Selmer corank is zero or one. The family also supplies analytic rank densities and their mean over twists, but an average or density-one assertion does not prove rank equality for every curve or every twist.  Rank013NP versus P/polyCan every yes-or-no problem with short, efficiently checkable evidence for yes answers be solved by Boolean circuits of polynomial size, if a separate circuit may be chosen for each input length? No efficient method of constructing those circuits is required.Theoretical computer scienceExact statement

Determine the truth of NP subseteq P/poly. Here NP consists of languages over finite binary strings accepted by nondeterministic Turing machines in polynomial time. P/poly consists of languages L for which there exist constants C>=1 and integer k>=1 and Boolean circuits C_n for all n>=0, of size at most C(n+1)^k, deciding membership in L on every length-n input. Circuits are finite acyclic single-output circuits with fan-in-two AND/OR, fan-in-one NOT, input bits and hardwired constants0/1; count all nodes. Each language has its own bound and circuit family, with no uniform generation requirement.

Why it matters

Containment would collapse the polynomial hierarchy to its second level by the Karp–Lipton theorem. Noncontainment would establish a general circuit-size barrier for an NP language and imply P ≠ NP.

StatusOpen

NP containment in nonuniform P/poly remains open; February 2026 notes pose the matching general-circuit question. Restricted circuits and Karp–Lipton implications do not decide it.

October 7, 2026: OpenAI’s October 6 release reports partial progress. The rank-equality theorem applies in particular to congruent-number curves y^2=x^3-n^2 x when a full q-power Selmer group has corank at most one; it then identifies whether their Mordell-Weil rank is zero or one. There is no unconditional classification of every squarefree n or a guarantee that every congruent-number curve meets the low-corank hypothesis. Congruent-number curves have rational two-torsion, so the companion identifies their actual rank when their full 2-power Selmer corank is zero or one. This does not decide congruence for every squarefree n: higher-corank twists and an exhaustive criterion are not covered. The low-corank 2-converse applies to those quadratic twists of y^2=x^3-x whose full 2-power Selmer corank is zero or one, giving the corresponding actual rank. Analytic densities and a mean over signed squarefree twists do not by themselves classify every individual positive congruent number. No independent proof audit or Lean verification was performed for this update.

Exact statement covered by this update

For every fixed pair of real constants epsilon, delta > 0 with epsilon + delta < 1, there exists an integer k >= 2, depending only on epsilon and delta, such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. An instance is a finite directed constraint graph G=(V,E) with E nonempty and, for each edge e=(v,w), a permutation pi_e of [k]. For a labeling L:V->[k], an edge is satisfied if pi_e(L(v))=L(w); val(G) is the largest fraction of satisfied edges over all labelings. Distinguish val(G) >= 1-epsilon from val(G) <= delta, with no requirement on instances between these thresholds. The graph is the growing input; epsilon, delta and k are fixed constants. NP-hardness means that every language in NP has such a reduction mapping yes inputs to the first promised set and no inputs to the second.

The word integrality in the title does not add an integral-valued requirement to the exact target, which asks membership in Q. Family 032: Theorem 1.1 proves rational algebraicity for every Hodge class in every codimension on every complex CM abelian variety. For the target CM variety over Q-bar, choose a complex embedding; its rational absolute Hodge class is in particular a rational Hodge class and therefore has a rational algebraic cycle representative. The usual descent/spreading of an algebraic representative to Q-bar and specialization at the chosen good reduction identify the reduced l-adic class with a specialized rational algebraic cycle. A Lefschetz class is, by the conventional definition, a rational combination of products of divisor classes on the reduced abelian variety, so it too is represented by a rational algebraic cycle. Their complementary-degree pairing is the degree of their intersection, a single rational number, and the cycle-class and specialization compatibilities identify that same number for every admissible l. The divisors defining the Lefschetz class need not lift to characteristic zero. Thus the stronger CM Hodge assertion supplies the target rationality and l-independence by this elementary cycle-class implication. The target asks membership in Q, not integrality in Z despite its inherited title.

entry.title: Lua for data representation (2025)
entry.content:
lua for data representation

my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]]. however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]). the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===], not with a ]] or a ]==], or a ]====].

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:

local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q, but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

anyway, download this file. if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

styles of data representationJSON style (LON?)

chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.

return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead. return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead. INI style

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

you can have a file like this:

-- config.lua foo = "bar" list = {1, 2, 3} rule_of_thirds = true then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this: local config = {} assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))() imperative style

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

path "/path/to/things" config { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } lipsum [[ Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda ]] programming in lua provides a real world example of this. security considerations

the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.

the main technique for sandboxing lua is controlling the environment. when using lua for data representation, an empty enivronment is the most appropriate (or, an environment that only exposes data constructors). this prevents any I/O or access to the larger program’s state. preventing access to all standard library functions is safest. there are a few standard library functions that have consequences you might not expect.

another concern is denial of service. this is trickier to prevent. it’s fairly trivial to construct a lua chunk which does not return (while true do end). debug.sethook can mitigate this somewhat. even so, it’s probably possible to construct something that uses excessive amounts of memory. that said, denial of service is significantly less problematic than the vulnerabilities that are completely avoided by depriving the untrusted code of any standard library functions.

finally, make sure to reject lua bytecode. untrusted lua bytecode is not safe and may cause arbitrary nasal demons in the lua interpreter. load can accept both bytecode and lua source by default. however, passing "t" for the mode parameter prevents this.

why?

clearly, it’s silly to bring in the entire lua interpreter where you would just use JSON or INI. where this use case of lua shines is when you’re already using lua for a project (and then you already have this powerful data description language), or when you need something with a lot of power or flexibility.

these mini languages can be extended to arbitrary complexity and nuance. unlike JSON, you can add arbitrary type constructors, or anything at all. you can build any kind of language you want, and that’s how lua is designed to be used, and it’s actually approximately the story of how it was invented.

if you’re anything like me, this will sound a little familiar. indeed, many have said similar things about lisp and forth. both of those languages have very different approaches but reach the same conclusion of “inventing your own language”. I believe lua belongs in their pantheon.

bonus content

python? js? ruby? what the hell are those? all I care about is LUA.
