entry.title: Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
entry.content:
Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native

Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.

More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.

Why the iOS Safari Experience Sucks

What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.

How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.

Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.

High Refresh Rate Interactions

Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.

If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.

In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.

Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed. Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region. Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container. Want a dial with notches? Snap points!

The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.

Creating “The Controller”

I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.

Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.

First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.

Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.

What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.

Each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.

Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering update queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.

This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.

I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.

Squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.

Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.

If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.

Just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.

One issue remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.

If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you can choose to invasively set the initial-scale in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.

From here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.

Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.

Breaking the 60 FPS Render Barrier

Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.

The vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?

Ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.

Asking Google yields the following preamble.

There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 <canvas> (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.

Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.

Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering update. Low Power Mode throttles further.

Well, as of today… you can!

At first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.

Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.

In WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.

Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.

Jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.

Putting it All Together

Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.

Applying Our Learnings

This page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.

When the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.

As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.

On this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.

After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.

Building a Tab Bar Component Building the Structure

Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.

Layout of Controllers

We’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.

Building the State Machine

We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the new events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.

If a controller is being touched we then magnify & lift the lens. We know where to move the lens based on the controller’s offset since the touch began. If the user pulls past the bounds of the tab bar, we stretch the bar towards their finger. Depending on the offset, when the user stops touching the controller, we settle the lens on the nearest tab. Adding razzle-dazzle

Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.

Performance

I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.

Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.

Wrapping Up

Liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!

Disclaimers

Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

entry.title: Macrohistory in Six Facts
entry.content:
Joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models. Economists often seem to forget that some of the most important theories in physics are either verified or refuted by a single observation, or a limited number of observations (e.g. Einstein’s theory of relativity, or the theory of black holes).”

Can we condense down the most important lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts? Here is one attempt: macrohistory in six (plus or minus) facts.

What I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences. On the Y-axis is life satisfaction, based on going around and asking people, ‘on a scale of zero to ten, how satisfied are you with your life’.

In richer countries, on average people are happier.

Or – in richer countries, on average people live longer:

Or – in richer countries, fewer babies die:

Are all these good things just coming from people working more? No – in richer countries, people work less; and as countries become richer over time, people work less:

More intangible things, too. You can ask people how much they trust their neighbors. In richer countries, people trust their neighbors more:

Of course, we know market capitalism has its flaws – for example, richer countries emit more CO2 per person:

And all of this is correlation not causation.

But we’re going to run with this, and use GDP per person as our measure of how well we are doing.

Which brings us to:

This is the most important fact about human history.

We are ∼10 times richer than our great-great-great grandparents, who themselves in turn were ∼2 times as rich as Jesus of Nazareth.

Everyone used to be poor. This is the most important fact about macro history.

Why did we used to be poor? We lived in a Malthusian hellscape:

This shows the real wage of workers in England since 1250.

Prior to the Industrial Revolution, any time wages rose, more babies would survive to adulthood, parents would have more babies, and the population would rise until wages were driven back to subsistence.

We lived in a Malthusian hellscape. Until:

The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in human history.

We went from 0.01% growth per year, up to 0.1% with the Industrial Revolution around 1750, to 1% with the Second Industrial Revolution around 1870, to the modern 2% growth rate.

The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in macro history. It also brought about:

The growth explosion from the Industrial Revolution did not take place everywhere and all at once. Many countries did not see faster growth and rising GDP per person until much later – and many still have not seen these much at all.

But let’s talk first about the frontier.

This is the most important fact in modern macro. Growth at the technological frontier – measured here as GDP per person in the United States – has been a shockingly steady 2% per year for the last 150 years.

You can see a temporary blip down for the Great Depression, but otherwise the trend has been remarkably constant.

Running water, electricity, automobiles, computers, the web – all show up here as a continuation of a steady 2% per year trend.

What about the rest of the world?

The figure here has on the X-axis, income per person per day. You can see, for example, that even the poorest 11% of people in the United States have on average a higher income than the median person in Bangladesh or Ethiopia.

Income varies enormously across countries. Those of us born in the United States are so, so lucky.

Well, are we stuck with these enormous differences? No:

Here again we see the United States up top as the frontier.

Japan and South Korea, at the turn of the 20th century, were ∼as poor as sub-Saharan Africa is today. But Japan and South Korea caught up close to the United States. There are growth miracles.

But there are also growth disasters. Argentina at the turn of the 20th century was one of the richest countries in the world. But it has stagnated, relative to the frontier. A classic basket case.

And there are countries like Nigeria, which have never experienced much sustained growth at all.

What should we expect of the future? This takes us to the most fun fact, the most speculative:

Over the long sweep of history, aggregate GDP growth is speeding up.

What I have plotted here is how long it takes for world GDP to double. This goes back to 1 million years ago. Measuring GDP in 1 million BC is hard, but for our purposes I feel good about these numbers.

We’ve gone from doubling every 100,000 years down to a modern doubling time of every 35 or so years.

———

Now, to the natural question: what should we expect about growth in the future?

I think it really comes down to: which prior do you want to anchor to?

Do you want to anchor to the last 150 years or so, with our constant 2% growth and doubling every 35 years?

Or do you want to anchor to the long sweep of macrohistory, where growth has been speeding up?

We live in a weird time.

Walking around outside, I think we should really feel bombarded with this fact, every day. All these buildings? All these people? All this stuff?

This is all kind of crazy. It’s all a little bonkers. Compared to the grand sweep of macrohistory, we live in a weird time.

I found these “Six Big Facts of Macrohistory” particularly useful as framing when teaching my undergrad macro course for the first time last fall: teaching GDP construction (fact 0), the Malthusian model (fact 1), the theories of the Industrial Revolution (fact 2), the Solow model (facts 3-5), and the endogenous growth model (fact 6).

It was pedagogically very useful to have this catechism of the Six Facts to review at the start of many classes, to anchor the students to where we were in the course.

It was also useful for me, for setting a target for the bare minimum that students might remember in a decade. Do I expect them to remember the capital accumulation equation of the Solow model? No. Or even the idea of income vs. substitution effects? For the vast majority – no, not really.

Can I hope that they pick up a gut-level sense, in their bones, that everyone used to be poor? That’s an extremely important idea, a realistic goal, and yet an idea that the vast majority of people do not know or have not properly internalized.

I also think the Six Big Facts of Macrohistory is a useful attempt to condense “what should any well-informed civilian know about macro and macrohistory”. E.g. my microeconomist wife, or my parents.

What are the runner-up facts not listed here? Structural transformation and urbanization? The demographic transition? Women’s emancipation or rising health would be the natural top candidates, but are captured (if perhaps buried) in Fact 0.

Again, underlying these figures is the astounding work of generations of economic historians, demographers, national statistical agencies, and others.

entry.title: Button Sounds – collection of professionally-recorded button clicks and presses
Serving Qwen via AWS Lambdas for fun and 80x negative profit
entry.content:
Serving Qwen via 5,600 Lambdas for fun and 80x negative profit Who needs a GPU?

In my work at Bevyl I was really impressed by the performance and cost characteristics of AWS Lambdas. They can massively distribute and fan out CPU-bound work, which is amazing for things like ffmpeg on long videos.

So I was curious if it was possible to run inference on self-hosted models using Lambdas. It was a random idea built on a hunch, and I like to prove such ideas right or wrong by building. In this case I was very wrong, but it was a good lesson!

I picked H2O-Lightning, a fine-tune of Qwen3.5-4B, because I wanted a small model built for decisions. I figured if this architecture had any legs, only doing decision models (a single forward pass) is the move. A decision model reads a document and answers a question about it by picking one option.

Fanning out

So the trick, if it's possible, would be fanning out. I was inspired how Remotion uses massively parallelized Lambdas to render videos.

I wanted to prove this was possible to do, so I kept a constraint of a 3 GB limit for Lambdas. The whole model is 9.3 GB, so it does not fit in one. But it has 32 layers of about 225 MB each, and one layer fits. That gave me one Lambda job per layer per block of tokens.

Think of the Lambda as a simple idempotent API. A job reads inputs from S3, does the math, and writes one object back.

x = load(f"{doc}/{layer - 1}/{block}") memory = load(f"{doc}/{layer}/{block - 1}") y, memory = model.layers[layer](x, memory) s3.put_object( Key=f"{doc}/{layer}/{block}", Body=pack(y, memory), )

Each job waits on the layer above for the same block and on its own previous block. Each layer starts one step after the layer above it, like a staircase 32 layers deep.

I'm proud of the win: splitting a model call across 5,600 Lambdas is kinda wild.

The bill

If it was 40x slower but 50% cheaper, that'd be interesting.

Reading a 4,000-token document takes 17 seconds and costs 3.4 cents. That works out to $8.40 per million tokens. Google sells a hosted decision model, Gemini Decision 1, for $0.10 per million tokens, so the same read costs 0.04 cents there. Mine is more than 80 times more expensive.

Takeaways Model engineering is not so hard in 2026!

I'm a dumb application developer, but I was able to play with model layers and transformers API pretty easily! With good devex, it feels like open models are just another API at this point.

I need a GPU

Learned this the hard way but a very powerful lesson! One layer over a few thousand tokens is a big matrix multiply, which is what GPUs are built for. My goal was to learn anyway so it's a good lesson.

Freedom ain't free

CPU still costs dollars, there's no arbitrage here.

entry.title: A faster algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of π
entry.content:
A faster algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of π

By Robert Smith

This post introduces a new algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of \(\pi\) without computing the preceding digits. It beats the standard term-by-term evaluations of Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP), Bellard, and Huvent on operation count. Even against Huvent’s eight-term formula, the savings are about 61% fewer divisions and 38% fewer full modular exponentiations.

The key insights come from the following identity:

The underlying series goes back to Euler, but has been rearranged to exploit more efficient evaluation. Collecting its terms by odd denominator lets us share the arithmetic in two places:

The common denominator \(M=2k+1\) means we can add four remainders and divide once. The surprise is that we don’t have to compute those remainders independently either. The gaps between the exponents are small multiples of \(k\) plus constants, so one starting power and the step \(2^k\bmod M\) let us reach the others by multiplication.

Two full exponentiations modulo \(3M\) serve both denominators \(M\) and \(3M\). That gives us up to eight powers of two, and we still only divide once.

Together, these two tricks save about a million full exponentiations per million hexadecimal places skipped compared with Huvent, before any machine-specific optimization. In practice, this algorithm leads to an implementation that runs in nearly 40% less wall-clock time.

The BBP trick and formula convergence

To see where the savings come from, let’s recall the BBP trick. To skip \(n\) hex digits, shift \(\pi\) left by \(d=4n\) bits and take the fractional part. Shifting by \(d\) bits adds \(d\) to each exponent, so we’re left adding and subtracting terms of the form \(2^E/N\). When \(E\ge 0\), write \(2^E=qN+r\). Then \(2^E/N=q+r/N\), and we don’t care about \(q\): it’s an integer. Even at \(d=4{,}000{,}000\), we can compute \(r=2^E\bmod N\) without ever constructing a four-million-bit numerator.

The terms with \(E<0\) make up the tail. They decay geometrically, so we sum them directly, keeping enough guard bits to settle the last digit we want.

The above is essentially the BBP trick, and is the basis for three decades of digit extraction algorithms.

As such, when I was programmatically looking for efficient BBP-formula, I ranked them by how many fractions I’d have to evaluate to reach a given digit. Each fraction in the main loop costs me a modular exponentiation and a division. Bellard’s formula advances 10 bits for every seven fractions; Huvent’s formula advances 12 bits for every eight. After finding Huvent’s formula independently, I’ve tried feverishly to find one with a better ratio, without success. So I looked toward ways of optimizing existing series.

One clue tipped me off. There’s a choice hiding in the last step of Bellard’s terse derivation. He has one sum in powers of \(1/4\) and another in powers of \(1/1024\). Since \(4^5=1024\), splitting the first sum into five progressions lets him write both sums in powers of \(1/1024\). What if, instead of lining up the powers, we lined up the denominators?

Lining up denominators

Lining up denominators seemed hard with the many-term series of Bellard and Huvent. One good place I found to try this is a series Euler wrote down in 1779, as noted by Craig-Wood, who used it himself to write an extraction program1. In Euler’s original formulation, there are six rows:

Takahashi writes this more straightforwardly as two sums distinguished by their exponential factors:

Notice the denominators of the fractions. Since \(4m+2=2(2m+1)\), we can halve the numerator of the middle fraction and leave \(2m+1\) in the denominator. As \(m\) runs over the nonnegative integers, \(2m+1\) gives every positive odd integer. The other two progressions, \(4m+1\) and \(4m+3\), split that same list between them. So each odd denominator appears twice in each sum.

For example, consider the denominator 13. The first progression hits it at \(m=3\); the middle one hits it at \(m=6\), where the original denominator was 26. That’s two contributions from the sum in powers of \(1/64\) and two from the sum in powers of \(1/1024\). The powers are different, but all four numerators can be added before we divide by 13. We can collect terms this way for every odd denominator.

To derive the boxed formula directly, we can start with a multiplication of Gaussian integers: \((3-i)^2(7-i)=50(1-i)\). Taking complex arguments gives Hutton’s arctangent identity from the 18th century:

Bellard lists this identity as equation (7). His logarithm trick works on both angles: \(1-(1+i)/4=(3-i)/4\), and \(1-(1+i)/8=(7-i)/8\). So if we put

then \(I_2=\arctan(1/3)\), \(I_3=\arctan(1/7)\), and we want \(\pi=8I_2+4I_3\). Every time \(j\) goes up by four, \((1+i)^j/2^{uj}\) is multiplied by \(-4/2^{4u}\). That’s \(-1/64\) in the first sum and \(-1/1024\) in the second.

For an odd denominator \(N=2k+1\), the two contributions in each logarithm come from \(j=N\) and \(j=2N\). All further doublings give multiples of four, where \((1+i)^j\) is real and contributes nothing. At \(j=N\) the imaginary part of \((1+i)^N\) is \((-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^k\); at \(j=2N\) we’re looking at \((2i)^N=(-1)^k 2^N i\). At \(j=N\), the first logarithm multiplies the imaginary part by \(8/2^{2(2k+1)}\), giving the numerator term \((-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^{1-3k}\). Collect the other three contributions in the same way and we have the boxed formula.

Four powers in two exponentiations

After the shift by \(d\), that is, multiplying the sum by \(2^d\), the four exponents, in the order we wrote them, are

Call a power active if its exponent is nonnegative. The slowest-decaying exponent is \(E_1\), which stays nonnegative up to \(k=\lfloor(d+1)/3\rfloor\). That’s about \(d/3\) odd denominators, and we divide just once for each one. Even the largest modulus is only \(2d/3+O(1)\), compared with about \(d\) for Bellard or Huvent, and \(2d\) for the original BBP formula.

As for the remainders \(r_j=2^{E_j}\bmod N\), notice that the middle two exponents differ by \(k\). If we already have \(r_3\) and \(x=2^k\bmod N\), then \(r_2\) is just \(xr_3\bmod N\). In fact, we can step from the smallest exponent up to the largest:

Start at the smallest active power. We pay for one full exponentiation to get it and one to get \(x\); the rest are a handful of multiplications. Past \(k\approx d/5\) only \(E_1\) is active, so don’t bother computing \(x\).2 That’s two exponentiations for the first \(d/5\) denominators and one for the remaining \(d/3-d/5\), or about \(8d/15\) altogether.

Two denominators for the price of one

So far we’ve paid for one division by 13 and another by 39. Call the signed sums of their active powers \(A\) and \(B\). Since 39 is three times 13, their combined contribution is

We only want the fractional part, so we can compute both numerators modulo 39, take the remainder of \(3A+B\), and divide by 39 just once.

Now consider the step powers. For 13 the index is 6; for 39 it’s 19. Since \(19=3\cdot6+1\), once we have \(x=2^6\bmod39\), we get the step for 39 by cubing and doubling: \(2^{19}\equiv2x^3\pmod{39}\).

In general, tripling a denominator \(M=2k+1\) changes its index from \(k\) to \(3k+1\). Substitute that index into the four exponents above to get the partner’s exponents. Now read the active exponents from both numerators in increasing order. The common \(d\) cancels in every gap, leaving a small multiple of \(k\) plus a constant. We need just two full exponentiations modulo \(3M\): one for the first power in the list and one for the step \(2^k\). Multiplication takes us up the rest of the list.

We never need to compute the step just for \(3M\). Its largest exponent, \(d-2-9k\), is smaller than the second exponent for \(M\), \(d-1-5k\). If \(3M\) has even one active power, \(M\) already has at least two.

We don’t want to pair 39 with 13 and then pair it again with 117. So we start pairs only at odd \(M\) not divisible by three. If \(3M\) has an active power, we take it with \(M\); otherwise we process \(M\) alone. Odd multiples of nine, like 117, stay unpaired.

The denominators that no longer need their own turn are precisely the odd multiples of three that aren’t multiples of nine. That’s two out of every nine odd denominators, both where we need one exponentiation and where we need two. Multiplying the counts above by \(7/9\) gives about \(7d/27\) divisions and \(56d/135\) full exponentiations, compared to \(2d/3\) of each for Huvent.

Here is how the formulas compare in terms of how far into \(\pi\) we get per expensive arithmetic operation, expressed as “bits per operation”:

Formula Bits per full mod. exp. Bits per division BBP, term by term 4/4 = 1.00 4/4 = 1.00 Euler, term by term 5/4 = 1.25 5/4 = 1.25 Bellard, term by term 10/7 ≈ 1.43 10/7 ≈ 1.43 Huvent, term by term 12/8 = 1.50 12/8 = 1.50 This post 135/56 ≈ 2.41 27/7 ≈ 3.86
Notes on a high-performance implementation

I implemented both the algorithm of this post and Huvent using AVX-512 IFMA. Here’s how long each took to extract 12 hex digits on my computer.

Hex digits skipped Threads Huvent (ms) This post (ms) % faster 1,000,000 1 8.09 4.88 +65.7% 100,000,000 1 962 584 +64.7% 1,000,000 32 4.23 3.82 +10.9% 100,000,000 32 64.4 42.4 +51.8% 1,000,000,000 32 655 410 +59.9% 1,000,000,000,000 32 845,685 520,907 +62.3%

Returning to the pair 13 and 39, while 39 is active, I never reduce modulo 13: changing the numerator for 13 by a multiple of 13 changes its tripled contribution by a multiple of 39. So I do all the squaring and multiplying modulo 39. Since 39 is odd, I can compute its inverse modulo a power of two once and reuse it for every Montgomery multiplication in the pair. I triple the numerator for 13, add the one for 39, and convert back from Montgomery form just once for the final division.

There’s a nice trick inside each exponentiation, too. Suppose a Montgomery reduction leaves \(-14\) modulo 39. Normally I’d add 39 to get 25. But if I’m going to square it next, 14 is just as good: \(14^2\equiv25^2\pmod{39}\). Even if the current exponent bit calls for doubling first, the next square still erases the sign. So for all but the last bit, I use vector absolute values instead of correcting the sign. On the last bit I do the usual reduction, since the numerator needs the actual residue rather than its negative. That change made the exponentiation loop about 8% faster on Zen 5.

Each vector lane handles a different odd modulus. I batch moduli with the same set of active powers so that one lane doesn’t sit idle while another steps through three extra residues. The hardware multiplies 52-bit inputs, so the largest modulus matters: ours is about \(2d/3\), compared with \(d\) for Huvent. That lets us reach about 50% farther into \(\pi\) before we need wider arithmetic.

I originally went looking for a series with fewer fractions per bit. If you evaluate every fraction separately, Euler’s series actually needs more fractions per bit than Huvent’s, so it has been easy to pass over. Sharing the modular arithmetic across common and paired denominators is what makes it faster, and I suspect similar tricks apply to other BBP-type series.

His implementation evaluates 21 fractions separately for every 30 bits of offset. ↩︎

There’s a way to thin out the far end of the loop even more. At \(j=4m+3\), the real and imaginary parts of \((1+i)^j\) are opposites. Add the real part of each logarithm and the two slow powers cancel for \(N\equiv3\pmod4\). We still have to subtract the real logarithms we added, using series for \(\log(1+2^{-2})\), \(\log(1+2^{-3})\), and \(\log(1-2^{-4})\). That leaves half as many moduli above \(d/2\), at the cost of more streams of powers to juggle below it. ↩︎

entry.title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, Stuff
entry.content:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.

Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.

Sponsorship update

It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.

SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.

The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction, possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations. Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos. Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately? I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from, how many users I have, or what they’re up to.

At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.

On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.

I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).

C++ Index…?

Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.

I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.

Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.

Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.

To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be massive, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.

Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.

I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.

Many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.

On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.

“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”

My friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult.

"${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!"

Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.

That said, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”âI don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convincedâif AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].

Even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. I’d be on the hook for an AI subscription perpetually hoping and praying the token prices wouldn’t ever go up. This is a nonstarter for the same reasons the search engine runs on its own hardware and not in the cloud. You can’t be truly independent if you’re subject to the whims of a landlord.

From a project management perspective, I’m not rushing anything to market. Project still has years of runway. I’m not beholden to any investors to deliver profits. Even if I wanted to, I have no employees to replace other than my self. What I would trade away is the very immersion in the problem domain that’s allowed me to get as far as I have with this project. What I’m expecting to be getting out of it is improved developer ergonomics and maybe a bit of performance if the aforementioned problem-immersion-thing pans out. That’s not something that brings me money, and something I can do because the project is in a fairly stable and mature state.

Thus, regardless of what happens in the future with AI, there isn’t an obvious opportunity cost to holding off.

Heck, let’s just consider popular future predictions about AI, where does this leave me?

AI bet pays of and models become exponentially more powerful, much cheaper, and ubiquitous like tap water: How shortsighted would it be to pay for crappy AI today when I could save my money and get exponentially better or more AI for the same dollars in the future? I’d have to really hate having money to do such a thing. OpenThropic IPOs, vocal shareholders from Ferenginar quite insistently ask where they money at, token prices go up singificantly: Only a problem if you’re dependent on AI. AI investment bubble crashes and it’s raining bankers like October 1929: Bad for everyone, but especially bad if you’re dependent on AI. Tech prists in SV chant binharic hymns as the Machine God emerges and the chosen of humanity transcends into the cyber rapture: Kind of orthogonal to whether I build this index port by hand. Zoomers decide that Kazcinski was right all along and instigate a Butlerian Jihad: Mostly a problem if you’re dependent on AI. Rise of the Machines, hydraulic press youtube channel stomping on a human face forever: Inconvenient regardless of choice of action.

[1] Lesser minds would think models outputting unmanitainable code is a sign of the superiority of AI. I’ll refer you to the most problematic prophet, Terry Davis, for that one.

[2] I used an m-dash aside in that paragraph. Anyone reckon mr robot wrote this? Discuss in groups.

entry.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
entry.content:
Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

Practical EIP takeover

To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.

To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.

Targets

We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.

Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.

Claiming Addresses

By default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.

With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:

Allocate 25 Elastic IPs in the current region. Store each address, checking for duplicates. Look up each address in the database. Keep and log any address that matches a target’s A record. Release every address that didn’t match. Move to the next region and repeat.

In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.

In just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.

The ban hammer

After 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions”. This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.

Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any issues, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?

We decided not to continue the full attack from the new account to avoid further abuse complaints, and instead decided to reach out to AWS with some suggestions that could make this attack less practical:

Introduce a new quota on the number of Elastic IPs that can be allocated per month. Using this kind of hard cap rate limit (which could be set to some reasonable amount for large organizations), the attack would be much less likely to succeed. Apply abuse restrictions at the organization level instead of at the account level. This would force an attacker to create a whole new organization each time they’re banned, which is more effort.

AWS has since responded. They informed us that they have no plans to change anything here. More on their response in the disclosure section below.

Real takeovers we found

Across our limited target list of bug bounty targets, we were able to claim and control 28 EIPs which matched a live DNS record in the scope, with almost half belonging to government bodies. Bear in mind, we only ran the automation for 48 hours, and we would likely have found more, had we continued.

The most notable were five US Treasury subdomains pointing to addresses we now controlled:

ftp.treasury.gov irssearch.treasury.gov pcp.treasury.gov rdgw.treasury.gov ww5.treasury.gov

We also got hits across a range of public bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, including a university, two government bodies, a financial services company, and a large networking vendor. The rest belonged to Intruder customers, who we reported to directly.

Impact

Once an attacker holds the IP behind a dangling DNS record, they have full control over what that subdomain serves. US government websites tell visitors they can trust a site if its domain ends in .gov and it uses HTTPS - so if an attacker successfully takes over a domain, their site passes the test and users would trust it without question. The attacker can even pass a certificate authority’s domain validation and get a trusted TLS certificate for the domain to make it look completely legitimate.

This legitimacy could lead to phishing using a convincing real government domain to steal users credentials. The attacker could also host services on that domain to gather incoming information, and steal data (e.g. credentials) from any old automations that still point at it. That’s particularly dangerous, since those credentials could provide immediate access to other systems not related to the initial takeover.

A subdomain which has been taken over can also interact with cookies scoped to its parent domain. If treasury.gov sets cookies with Domain=treasury.gov, they are sent to every subdomain, including ones an attacker controls, which could enable session theft in other treasury.gov applications.

How practical is it?

AWS publishes 80 million IPv4 addresses for EC2, and our 450,000 allocated IPs cover 0.56% of that space. At our rate of about 9,400 IP addresses per hour, one account would take a year to cycle through every published address.

That’s slow for an attacker with one account. With multiple accounts, it comes down quickly. If bans really do apply only per account, as our experience suggests, 10 accounts could sweep the full space in around five weeks.

Realistically, the acquirable space is much smaller. Much of it is made up of auto-assigned public IPs or addresses held long-term by other customers, so a real sweep would take less time than these figures suggest.

An opportunistic attacker doesn’t need to cover the whole space to find something worth having. Even at 0.56% coverage, we landed 28 subdomains.

Targeting a specific organization narrows the search. An attacker would start by enumerating the target’s subdomains and identifying records that point to unused EC2 addresses. As AWS publishes the region of each range, they can look up exactly which region to search. For a target in eu-west-2, that’s around 2.2 million addresses rather than 80 million. However, when we allocated repeatedly in the same region, we saw a much higher duplicate rate, slowing the search. A targeted attacker therefore has a smaller haystack, but a slower way of searching it.

Responsible disclosure

All findings were reported through the relevant bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, and affected Intruder customers were contacted directly. We also shared our observations on the abuse controls with AWS.

AWS confirmed with us that they don’t plan to make changes, as they see the takeover as depending on customer-side DNS records rather than an issue in their services. They also told us they treat rapid allocation and release as a policy violation and have controls against it. Whilst this is true, they could do more to prevent the issue in our opinion, and the vulnerability class remains open due to their position.

Timeline Enumerated Elastic IPs - 23rd August Submitted findings to bug bounty programs - 25th August Reached out to AWS - 8th October Received an initial response from AWS - 8th October Followed up with AWS - 10th November AWS confirmed no plans to fix - 17th November Post published - 24th November

entry.title: Windows Loudness Equalization, reverse-engineered and ported to PipeWire
entry.content:
Windows' Loudness Equalization for PipeWire, reverse engineered from WMALFXGFXDSP.dll. It evens out the volume of each application, so quiet and loud parts play at a similar level.

modules/loudness/: the PipeWire module and the DSP plugin. It processes every app's playback stream. modules/limiter/: the output limiter of Windows' audio engine (AudioEng.dll), on every playback device. It keeps the boost from clipping. app/: an optional window (GTK3) to turn it on or off, globally or per app, and set the release time.

Requires PipeWire ≥ 1.4, and GTK 3 for the window.

# Arch: sudo pacman -S pipewire gtk3 pkgconf make gcc # Debian: sudo apt install libpipewire-0.3-dev libspa-0.2-dev libgtk-3-dev pkg-config make gcc make sudo make install systemctl --user restart pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber

To install only one part, use make -C modules/loudness, make -C modules/limiter or make -C app. To uninstall, run sudo make uninstall and restart the same services.

Open Loudness Equalization from your application menu, or run pw-loudness-eq.

The settings live in a PipeWire metadata object, so they can also be scripted:

pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 enabled false # turn off pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 release 6 # release time, 2 (fast) to 7 (slow) pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 disabled-apps '["Discord"]' Spa:String:JSON # leave these apps alone pw-metadata -n loudness-eq # show settings

Changes apply immediately and are kept across restarts.

Defaults are in /usr/share/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/60-loudness-eq.conf. To override them, copy it to ~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/.

Arg Default enabled true Start enabled release 4 Windows "Release Time", 2 (fast) to 7 (slow). 4 is the Windows default stream.rules Never process some apps: [ { matches = [ { application.name = "Discord" } ] actions = { loudness-eq = false } } ]

Settings changed at runtime are saved in ~/.local/state/pw-loudness-eq/state.conf and take precedence over this file.

The loudness module sets audioconvert.filter-graph.90 on each app's playback stream, so the plugin runs inside that stream, before its volume and before mixing, like a Windows stream effect.

The limiter module does what Windows' audio engine does on every playback device: after the mix and the software volume, it runs the output through a look-ahead limiter. It's always on, independent of Loudness Equalization, as on Windows.

Not processed: JACK clients, streams with more than 8 channels, and Flatpak apps that use PipeWire directly (those going through PulseAudio are processed).

A broadband automatic gain control. Despite the name, it doesn't equalize the spectrum.

Frame size N = 2^⌈log2(fs/100)⌉ (512 at 44.1/48 kHz), with 50% overlap. Each channel is windowed with w[n] = 16384·(1 − cos(2π(n+½)/N)) / (N/2) and run through a real FFT to get the power spectrum. Power is summed into 25 bands with edges at 100, 200, 300, 400, 510, 630, 770, 920, 1080, 1270, 1480, 1720, 2000, 2320, 2700, 3150, 3700, 4400, 5300, 6400, 7700, 9500, 12000, 15500 and 24000 Hz. Channels are summed together. Loudness L = 1.72 · Σ max(E_b − T_b, 1e-32)^0.25, with T = 1000, 100, 31.6, 10, 3.16, 2, 1, 1, .316, .316, 1×11, 4, 10, 100, 1000. Target gain = min((1300/L)^1.6, 10), so at most +20 dB. When the target is lower than the current gain, the gain jumps to it instantly. Otherwise it moves toward it by w = (N/128)·(44100/fs)·0.1^min(r,3)·0.316^(min(r,7)−min(r,3)) per block. At r = 4 that's a time constant of about 4.6 s. The gain is crossfaded linearly across each half-frame. Latency is N samples.

The boost can push pure tones such as a whistle well above full scale; the limiter catches that.

Ported from CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dll. audiodg.exe puts it on every render device, after its effects, before the device.

The output is delayed by L frames (64 at 44.1/48 kHz; 16, 32 or 128 at other rates) to look ahead. That's the device's added latency. When a frame entering the delay peaks above the tracked peak (initially 0.985), the gain ramps down linearly over those L frames to 0.985 / peak, reaching it as that frame leaves. All channels share one gain. The gain only recovers once the signal peaks at half the tracked peak or less: it rises by e^(2.205/fs) per frame (about 19 dB/s) while the tracked peak decays by the same factor.

On Windows the device's software volume comes before the limiter; in PipeWire it comes after the device's filter graphs. So the plugin gets the volume of each channel (kept in sync by the module), measures peaks on the signal as it will be after the volume, and applies only its gain. Once PipeWire applies the volume, the result is the same as Windows'. Hardware volume comes after the limiter on both.

make check # DSP and plugin tests, both modules modules/loudness/build/leq-wav [-r release] in.wav out.wav # process a file offline

entry.title: Hazel (YC W24) Is Hiring a Product Designer
entry.content:
AI-enabled procurement for government

Our mission at Hazel is simple and powerful. We use AI to help U.S. government purchasing teams buy at the speed of need with unparalleled efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is a $2.7T problem every single year, and Hazel is at the forefront with Federal and State, Local, and Education (SLED) agencies.

Hazel has identified a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to solve this by deploying cutting-edge AI to the public sector and unlocking the full potential of our nation. We empower our partners to move with expediency against the most pressing challenges of this century. Hazel builds AI for the public interest.

Hazel is transforming government procurement: how government agencies purchase goods and services from commercial vendors. Our federal partners use our AI-forward bid evaluations solution to assess vendors more accurately, reliably, and quickly. With the federal government under increasing pressure to accelerate acquisitions, our tools give them a real edge.

Our COTS products, led by Document Builder and Evaluations, serve state & local governments, schools, and special authorities. The users are procurement officers working through long, high-stakes documents and decisions, and they deserve software that is as clear and trustworthy as it is powerful.

As Hazel's contract Product Designer, you will elevate the user experience and visual design of products government teams rely on daily. Hazel has built a substantial product based on deep understanding of our users' needs. In this role, you will refine our UI/UX and establish standards for our engineering team going forward.

There are three main deliverables:

Federal. Upgrade the UI/UX of the bid evaluations solution we are deploying for our largest federal contract.

Commercial. Improve the UX of our COTS product flows and define consistent UI elements to unify the product design.

Playbook. Deliver a practical style guide and Figma component set so Hazel engineers can ship consistent, high-quality UI after the engagement ends.

Audit Hazel's existing workflows and identify the highest-impact UI/UX improvements

Design high-fidelity screens, flows, and interaction states for complex, document-heavy workflows, including how users review and act on AI output

Work directly with Hazel's founders and engineers, sharing work early and iterating quickly

Hand off production-ready designs and review what ships to ensure quality

Build a reusable set of Figma components and documented patterns

Write a practical style guide our engineers can follow for new features, including accessibility basics (Section 508 / WCAG 2.1 AA)

Proven experience as a product designer or similar role, with a portfolio of shipped work

Strong skills across UI/UX

Experience designing complex, workflow-heavy B2B applications (dense tables, long forms, multi-step reviews and approvals)

Experience working within and contributing to a design system

Ability to improve an existing product without starting from scratch

Fast turnaround and independence: you ship in days, not weeks

Expert in Figma or similar tools

Excitement about bringing innovation to the public sector

Has worked at a startup or startup-like environment

Building a design system from scratch and documenting it for others

Front-end coding experience (React, TypeScript)

Designing AI features, including surfacing sources and letting users review and correct model output

Document-centric interfaces: reading, annotating, or comparing long documents

Working with or adjacent to the public sector

Accessibility work to Section 508 or WCAG 2.1 AA

Federal acquisition or source selection

$10,000 - $20,000/month depending on experience | Contract for 3-6 months, 20-40 hrs/week

Remote, with potential working sessions in person with the team. All travel expenses will be paid.

U.S. Citizenship required

Opportunity for future projects or a longer-term role

You will set the design standard for Hazel. Your work will ship to federal evaluators and to procurement teams across states, cities, and schools. The style guide you leave behind will shape every feature we build after.

You'll work side-by-side with inquisitive and driven founders as well as a world-class and dynamic founding engineering team, with frontline exposure to our government partners.

Hazel is a mission-driven organization founded by engineers and built around delivering world-class innovation to our government partners. We strive for excellence, deliver impact, and have fun doing it.

You care about mission. Hazel partners with agencies supporting everything from public school teachers in the classroom to warfighters in the field. We believe in products which change America for the better.

You want a startup that is structured without being rigid, quality-obsessed without being slow, and product-led without losing the vision. You take ownership: shaping the experience, talking to customers, and wearing many hats.

You solve problems. There's no more time to opine on strategy and policy when our nation faces existential challenges, today. We are workhorses, not showhorses.

You are always learning. Nobody has all the answers, and the world is ever-evolving, so we must be adaptive. We bring the best practices available from all domains to meet the challenge.

You believe in team. Our team grows together, supports one another, and elevates our shared successes. We are more effective together.

Our mission at Hazel is simple and powerful. We use AI to help U.S. government purchasing teams buy at the speed of need with unparalleled efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is a $2.7T problem every single year, and Hazel is at the forefront with State, Local, and EDucation (SLED) and federal government agencies.

Government procurement has moved at a glacial pace for decades, stovepiped by complex processes, regulatory capture, and overworked civil servants. The impacts are severe. Our founders saw at Palantir and BCG how lowly procurement challenges fueled wildfires across California, compromised critical U.S. national security systems, and wasted billions of dollars.

Hazel has identified a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to solve this by deploying cutting-edge AI to the public sector and unlocking the full potential of our nation. We empower our partners to move with expediency against the most pressing challenges of this century including climate sustainability, great power competition, and more. Hazel builds AI for the public interest. The founders August and Elton saw this problem firsthand at Palantir and BCG, and they have enlisted a deep bench of investors from both tech and government to deploy one of the first real commercial applications of generative AI in the public sector.
